To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the best feature set for a relation extraction task is the combination of features of all three complexity levels, and the features from all three sentence representation types.

(1) a simple combination of basic unit features from different sentence representations gives the best performance, and (2) the inclusion of complex features does not necessarily help, but the combination of features from different levels of complexity does.

(i) using only basic unit feature is generally sufficient to obtain state-of-the-art results, (ii) overinclusion of more complex features may hurt performance, (iii) a combination of features of various levels of complexity, coupled with task-specific feature pruning, gives best performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the feature selection problem for relation extraction and provides some useful guidelines for feature selection in relation extraction.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the performance of a relation extraction system is mainly determined by the features of the relation instances and the feature selection method used, rather than the sentence representation.
a large space of feature subspaces can be explored for relation extraction, but only a small subset of features is actually needed.
, for relation extraction, it is not the number of features that matters, but the right combination. 1
The main takeaway from our work is that
a systematic exploration of a large space of feature spaces can be used to find an optimal feature space that achieves state-of-the-art results.
, for the relation extraction problem, the feature space is not infinite, but rather a large, finite space.
, for a task like relation extraction, a good feature space is not necessarily a big one, and a good classifier is not necessarily a complex one.
